Where is Joliet, Illinois, and how is the city laid out?

Joliet serves as Will County's seat of government, about 40 miles southwest of Chicago, and a small part of the city lies in Kendall County. The 2020 census counted 150,362 people, which made it the third most populous city in Illinois, and the Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate is 152,241.

The city has an irregular, sprawling shape that reaches into nine townships, more than any other Illinois city: Joliet, Plainfield, Troy, New Lenox, Jackson, Channahon and Lockport in Will County, and Na-Au-Say and Seward in Kendall County. It grew along the Des Plaines River, and locals speak of an east side and a west side relative to the river, plus a far west side that includes the Kendall County land.

That patchwork has a practical result. Your address may sit in a different school district, assessor's office and tax bill from a neighbor a few blocks away, so check the parcel before assuming anything.

What is Joliet's history, and what does it mean for older houses?

Joliet was settled in 1833 and reincorporated as a city in 1852. Joliet Iron and Steel Works ran from 1869 to 1936 and was once the second largest steel mill in the country. The old prison, completed in 1858 from local limestone, closed in 2002 and has offered tours since 2018. U.S. Route 66 runs through town, and the first Dairy Queen opened here.

Housing history left its mark. During the 1930s many owners could not keep up their large houses, and in the 1940s big Victorian homes were divided to house several families. Absentee landlords and deferred maintenance followed, and heavy use of vinyl siding changed several historic limestone buildings. The Joliet East Side Historic District, created in 1980, and the Upper Bluff Historic District, created in 1991, are both listed on the federal historic register.

  • If your house stands in one of those districts, ask the city's Planning and Zoning staff what review applies before you plan repairs.
  • If a large older house was ever split into units, bring any records of that conversion.
  • Buyers of pre-war houses commonly ask about foundations and wiring, so have repair records ready.

What do the Census numbers show for Joliet homeowners?

QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 shows 73.7 percent of homes owner-occupied, with a median home value of $265,800 among them, and 51,055 households averaging 2.89 people. Median gross rent is $1,276, the median household income is $92,201, and 11.1 percent of residents are in poverty. About 91.1 percent had not moved in the past year, and the mean commute is 28.8 minutes.

Homeowners with a mortgage had median monthly owner costs of $1,960, compared with $819 for owners with no mortgage.

  • About 26.3 percent of homes are not owner-occupied, so landlords and tenants figure in many Joliet sales.
  • Only 11.5 percent of residents are 65 or older, and 24.4 percent are under 18.
  • With 34.2 percent Hispanic or Latino residents and 28.8 percent speaking another language at home, bilingual paperwork can be useful.

What jobs, schools and roads shape the Joliet housing market?

Joliet has moved from a steel and manufacturing town to a commuter city. Downtown draws on the Rialto Square Theatre, the Joliet Slammers' ballpark and two casinos, and the largest employers in the city's 2017 financial report included Amazon, a Joliet hospital, Will County, Joliet Junior College and the public school districts.

The motto Crossroads of Mid-America on the city seal points to the meeting of I-80 and I-55 near Channahon. US 6, US 30, US 52 and US 66 also cross the city, as do Illinois Routes 7, 53, 59 and 171. The Joliet Transportation Center is the final stop for the Metra Heritage Corridor and Rock Island District lines, and Amtrak stops at Joliet Union Station. Pace buses leave a downtown terminal about once an hour, six days a week.

Schools vary by address. Joliet Public School District 86 and several smaller districts feed Joliet Township High School District 204. Other parts of the city fall in Plainfield District 202, New Lenox District 122 and, in Kendall County, Minooka and Oswego districts. Joliet Junior College and the University of St. Francis are the local colleges.

What does the City of Joliet require before a house sells?

The seller of residential or commercial property inside city limits buys the transfer tax stamp. The city prints the cost as $3.00 per $1,000 of purchase price. The stamp applies only to incorporated Joliet, and the city offers an address verification map and a phone line for borderline addresses.

  • A completed water and lien letter must reach the city at least four business days before closing. Forms received later may not be processed before the closing date.
  • An exempt stamp, with no charge, is needed on any deed change inside city limits, such as adding or removing a name, moving a property into or out of a trust, or a divorce.
  • Exempt stamps require the original signed and notarized deed, not a copy, with exempt language on it or a completed city exemption form.
  • Start or stop water service through Customer Service at 815-724-3820, option 2.

Questions about stamps go to the Customer Service real estate transfer stamps desk at 815-724-3902. Joliet's FAQ also says most exterior projects, including fences, decks, pools, patios, garages, additions and concrete work, need a building permit and a plat of survey, so look for those before you list.

How is a deed recorded in Will County, and what does it cost?

The Will County Recorder of Deeds is at 158 N. Scott Street in Joliet, phone 815-740-4637. Its fee schedule effective October 1, 2025 lists $90.00 for a standard document and $118.00 for a non-standard one. A standard document stays within up to five property index number references and up to five related document references.

The Recorder's guidelines list what a deed needs: a notarized original deed, grantee name and address, a tax bill-to name and address, a property address, a permanent index number, the real estate transfer tax declaration or exemption, and the municipal transfer tax stamp. Joliet is one of nine Will County municipalities that require that stamp.

The state tax comes from 35 ILCS 200/31-10. Ask the title company for the county portion and the total due at closing.

Which Joliet property tax and rental rules should a seller know?

Joliet's FAQ sends Will County owners to the Will County Treasurer's Office or the Supervisor of Assessments for tax bills, homestead exemptions and appeals, and Kendall County owners to the Kendall County Treasurer and Assessment Office. The back of your property tax bill lists your township assessor's contact.

If the house is a rental, the city runs a Rental Inspection Program with an owner registration form, a landlord checklist and a fee schedule. Ask Neighborhood Services at 815-724-4090 whether the property is registered before you tell a buyer anything about it.

The city also bans parking on streets automatically when 2 inches or more of snow falls within 24 hours, under City Code Sec. 19-142, and prohibits boats, RVs, trailers and trucks over 8,000 pounds on streets and in residential parkways. Buyers who own a trailer or boat will ask about both.

What are the realistic ways to sell a Joliet house fast?

Each option suits a different situation.

  • List with an agent. A house in good repair does well on the open market.
  • Sell on your own. You handle the contract, the city stamp and the water and lien letter yourself.
  • Accept a cash offer. It can fit an inherited house, a rental with tenants or a property with a failed inspection, and closing can follow the schedule you need.

Work backward from closing. The water and lien letter is due four business days ahead, the stamp must be bought before recording, and the deed must be the original. Missing any one of them can push a closing back.

The Census Bureau estimated 152,241 residents on July 1, 2025. The 2020 census counted 150,362.

How much is the Joliet transfer stamp?

The city prints $3.00 per $1,000 of purchase price, and the seller buys the stamp. Exempt stamps carry no charge.

How early must the water and lien letter reach the City of Joliet?

At least four business days before closing. Forms received later than that may not be processed before the closing date.

Where do I record a deed for a Joliet house?

Joliet is the Will County seat, so deeds go to the Will County Recorder of Deeds at 158 N. Scott Street. The fee schedule effective October 1, 2025 lists $90.00 for a standard document.

Does a Joliet house in Kendall County use a different office?

Yes. A small part of Joliet is in Kendall County, so that parcel's tax bill and deed run through Kendall County offices. The city's address verification map and the tax bill show which county applies.

What is Peoria's history and layout?

Peoria was the earliest permanent European settlement in what became Illinois. French explorers built Fort Crevecoeur here in 1680, Fort Clark followed in 1813, and the town took the name Peoria when the county was organized in 1825. It became a village in 1835 and a city in 1845.

The city covers about 48 square miles of land, and its neighborhoods include Downtown, the East Bluff, the West Bluff, the Uplands, Moss-Bradley, North Valley, Northwest Peoria, the Heart of Peoria, University East, and the Glen Oak-Flanagan and Randolph-Roanoke historic districts. Several of those areas, such as Averyville and El Vista, began as separate unincorporated towns that the city absorbed, so a Peoria sale can look very different from one neighborhood to the next.

How big is the Peoria housing market, and who lives there?

The Census Bureau counted 113,150 residents in 2020 and estimated 110,920 for July 2025, a drop of 2.0 percent from the 2020 base. Pekin, across the river, has about 31,000.

Only 57.5 percent of units are owner-occupied, so a large landlord and investor base is part of the market, and the city has rules for properties that owners do not live in, covered below.

What jobs and hospitals drive demand in Peoria?

Health care leads. OSF HealthCare has been the top employer since 2021 and moved its headquarters into a renovated downtown building in 2022. It opened a $250 million cancer institute in February 2024. Carle Health completed its purchase of Methodist and Proctor hospitals from UnityPoint in 2023 and is the third-largest employer.

Industry still matters:

  • Caterpillar Tractor Co. was formed in 1925, kept its world headquarters in Peoria for over 110 years, and remains the second-biggest employer even though the headquarters moved to Deerfield after a late 2017 announcement.
  • Komatsu America builds off-highway trucks in Peoria and announced a new office building in September 2024.
  • Bradley University, Methodist College, the OSF St. Francis College of Nursing, the University of Illinois College of Medicine at Peoria and Illinois Central College's north campus are based in the city.

The hospitals cluster in a medical district near Interstate 74 and Knoxville Avenue, southeast of downtown.

Which roads and school districts matter for a Peoria address?

Interstate 74 runs through downtown and crosses the river on the Murray Baker Bridge. Interstate 474 forms a southern bypass, and Interstate 155 runs south from Morton toward Lincoln. Illinois Routes 6, 8, 29 and 40 and U.S. Route 150 serve the city itself.

Several school districts cover the city:

  • Peoria Public Schools District 150 serves most of it, with Richwoods, Manual and Peoria High School, the oldest high school in Illinois.
  • Dunlap Community Unit School District 323 serves the far north and northwest.
  • Pleasant Valley School District 62, Limestone Community High School District 310, Peoria Heights District 325 and Illinois Valley Central District 321 cover edge areas.

Because a few blocks can change a child's district, give buyers the district name that matches the address.

How does Peoria's weather affect older houses?

Peoria has a humid continental climate. Precipitation averages about 36 inches a year and snowfall about 26.3 inches. The recorded extremes run from minus 27 degrees in January 1884 to 113 degrees in July 1936, and the 1991 to 2020 normals put July afternoons near 86 degrees and January afternoons near 34.

Swings that wide are hard on older roofs, flashing, chimneys and basement walls. A buyer's inspector will ask how old the roof, chimney and basement walls are and when they were last repaired. Collect receipts and permit records before you list.

What must you do with a Peoria rental or vacant property?

The city requires registration of rental properties, vacant residential properties and any dwelling the owner does not live in. Owners renew by February 28 each year. A new registration is due within 30 days after closing or after the home becomes non-owner occupied.

Fees listed by the city:

  • Renewal for a single-family home is $75; a multi-family property pays $75 for the first unit and $20 for each additional unit.
  • New single-family registrations cost $75 from January 1 to September 30 and $50 from October 1 to December 31.
  • A late registration fee of $150 per property applies after February 28 or more than 30 days after purchase.

You can register as exempt when the property is vacant and for sale, with an MLS or other listing as proof, when it is in probate or estate settlement, when an immediate family member lives there, when it holds a city Mothball Permit, or when an owner-occupied home is temporarily vacant for up to six months. Owners who live outside Peoria, Tazewell and Woodford counties must appoint a local property manager. Tell the city if you sell or buy a property, and use the Change of Status form to deactivate a sold property's registration.

What does the Peoria transfer declaration require at closing?

The City of Peoria's real estate transfer declaration prints a tax of $2.50 per $1,000 of consideration or part thereof. It also asks you to check whether the property will be owner occupied or non-owner occupied. If the non-owner box is checked, section 5-522(a) of the city code requires the property to be registered as non-owner occupied at the time of closing.

The form lists exemptions, including deeds where the actual consideration is less than $100, tax deeds, deeds that only confirm or correct a prior recorded deed, and deeds to or from governmental bodies. The county side runs separately: Peoria County takes part in the state MyDec system, which allows the PTAX-203 to be submitted electronically before the deed is recorded. Ask your closing attorney or title company to prepare the city form with the county filing so nothing holds up the recording.

How can you sell a Peoria house fast?

With a median value of $156,200 and a large rental share, a house that needs work often sells to an investor. Those buyers pay cash, close on your schedule and buy as-is, while a listed sale usually means repairs, showings and a lender's appraisal.

  • Decide whether the house is owner occupied, vacant or rented, since that sets the registration steps.
  • Collect the deed, tax bills and any code notices.
  • Compare a cash offer to a listing by what you net after repairs and carrying costs.

More questions about Peoria, IL

How much is the City of Peoria real estate transfer tax?

The city's transfer declaration prints $2.50 per $1,000 of consideration or part thereof. The form includes a list of exempt deed types. Ask your closing attorney to complete it with the PTAX-203 filed through the county.

Do I have to register a Peoria house I am selling?

Only if it is not owner occupied. Vacant homes listed for sale qualify for an exempt registration when you give the city an MLS or other listing as proof. After a sale, tell the city and use the Change of Status form to deactivate the registration.

When is Peoria's non-owner-occupied registration due?

Renewals are due every year by February 28, and new properties must be registered within 30 days after closing or after becoming non-owner occupied. A $150 late fee applies after those dates.

Which school district is my Peoria house in?

Most of Peoria is in District 150, but Dunlap District 323, Pleasant Valley District 62, Limestone District 310, Peoria Heights District 325 and Illinois Valley Central District 321 cover other parts. Check the address with the district before you list.

Is Peoria a good market for a quick cash sale?

A cash sale is an option for many houses. Only 57.5 percent of units are owner occupied, so investors and landlords are part of the buyer pool. Compare any offer against a listed sale after repairs, fees and carrying costs.

Schaumburg homeowners can move fast by pricing a listing to sell, by selling privately, or by accepting a direct purchase from a buyer who closes with cash. The direct sale trims the most time, since it skips repairs, staging and the weeks a lender needs. What cannot be skipped is the village's transfer stamp, which gates the closing in Schaumburg.

The sections below cover the village itself, the numbers buyers see, and the local steps for vacant homes, water service and transfer taxes.

What should a seller know about Schaumburg itself?

Schaumburg is a village in Cook and DuPage counties, about 26 miles northwest of downtown Chicago and 10 miles northwest of O'Hare International Airport. At the 2020 census it had 78,723 residents, which made it the most populous incorporated village in the United States. It covers about 19.5 square miles and was incorporated on March 7, 1956.

Growth came fast. The O'Hare opening in 1955 and the Northwest Tollway in 1956 improved access, then Alfred Campanelli began the Weathersfield subdivision in 1959 and eventually built more than 6,800 housing units. Woodfield Mall opened in 1971. Most of the village was built out between the 1960s and the 1990s, so many Schaumburg sellers are selling a house or unit with decades of wear on its roof, windows and mechanicals.

The Olde Schaumburg Centre Overlay District, set up in 1978, protects the historic area around Schaumburg and Roselle Roads.

What do Census numbers show for Schaumburg housing?

Census QuickFacts puts Schaumburg at 77,249 residents on July 1, 2025, with 31,655 households averaging 2.41 people from 2020 to 2024. Only 62.9% of housing units are owner-occupied, so renters make up a large share of the village.

The village website lists Woodfield Mall as the top employer at 4,400 workers, followed by Zurich North America at 2,600, Motorola Solutions at 1,600 and OptumRx at 1,300, with IBM, Genworth Financial and Paylocity also on the list. Private options in the village include Schaumburg Christian School, St. Peter Lutheran School and St. Hubert Catholic School. Roosevelt University has a Schaumburg campus in the former Pure Oil headquarters building, and the Schaumburg Township District Library has its main branch here. Not every District 54 school sits inside the village, so check the attendance boundary for the address you are selling.

Schaumburg ties its transfer stamp to the condition of vacant homes. If the inspection finds violations that are not corrected, the buyer must provide a notarized letter of intent before the stamp is released. Other holds on the stamp for the property must also be cleared first. Questions go to the Building Division at 847-923-4420.

Vacant homes must also be registered under Chapter 123.04 of the Village Code. There is no registration fee. Minimum upkeep includes cutting grass before it passes eight inches, removing dead shrubs, clearing accumulated mail and notices, replacing broken windows or doors, keeping sump pumps working and weatherizing the property. Code Enforcement can be reached at 847-923-3700.

It depends on the parcel, because Schaumburg lies in both Cook and DuPage counties. Check the parcel number, then file with that county's recording office along with the required state and county stamps.

What kind of village is Skokie?

Skokie is a village in Cook County, in Niles Township, about 15 miles north of the Chicago Loop. It covers roughly 10 square miles and borders Evanston, Chicago, Lincolnwood, Niles, Morton Grove, Glenview and Wilmette. Its street grid continues Chicago's numbering, which is why house numbers here read like Chicago addresses.

The community was incorporated in 1888 as Niles Centre, and voters picked the name Skokie in a referendum on November 15, 1940. The 1920s brought subdivisions of two and three flats and the Chicago-style bungalow, and a second building wave followed in the 1940s and 1950s. That history explains why so many Skokie homes are brick bungalows and mid-century houses, a stock that tends to need updated kitchens, electrical panels and mechanicals.

Major east-west roads include Old Orchard Road, Golf Road, Dempster Street, Oakton Street and Touhy Avenue, with Skokie Boulevard, Crawford Avenue and McCormick Boulevard running north and south.

The Illinois Science and Technology Park occupies the former Pfizer laboratories downtown, and Westfield Old Orchard is one of the larger malls in Illinois. Buyers who work in those places, or commute by Yellow Line, are the people most likely to pay a premium for a renovated Skokie house.

Because the boundary depends on the street, confirm the district for a specific address before you advertise schools to a buyer.

The village also hosts Oakton College's Ray Hartstein Campus on Lincoln Avenue and Hebrew Theological College on Carpenter Road. Skokie has many religious day schools alongside the public districts, and the village's Jewish community has been part of its identity since the post-war decades.

To process the stamp, submit the completed Real Estate Transfer Tax Form together with a Request for Final Water Reading. The request lists the closing date, a contact name, phone and email, the seller's forwarding address for the last water bill, and the buyer's phone and email. Documents can go to transfertax@skokie.org or by mail to the Clerk's Office. The clerk's phone is 847-933-8203.

There is one more step for rental property. Cook County bills Skokie parcels in two installments. Tax year 2024 was due March 4, 2025 and December 15, 2025, and tax year 2023 was due March 1, 2024 and August 1, 2024. The schedule has shifted from year to year, so ask the Treasurer for the current installment dates and any payment already posted to your parcel.

At closing, the title company usually divides the year's tax between buyer and seller by closing date. Exemptions also matter: the Treasurer's site lists a Homeowner Exemption, a Senior Citizen Homestead Exemption and a Senior Citizen Assessment Freeze Exemption, and a buyer needs to apply for the ones they qualify for after the sale.

You can sell it, but the village will not issue the transfer stamp while code violations or village balances remain open. Clear them first, or ask the Clerk's Office at 847-933-8203 how an open item affects your closing.

Growth came in waves. The village was founded in 1866 around a station on the Chicago and North Western Railway. After World War II the first suburb-style subdivision, Palanois Park, went up, and the population climbed from 11,504 in 1960 to 26,050 in 1970 and 65,479 by 2000. So much of the village's housing was built in the decades after 1950, and buyers of houses that age tend to ask about roofs, furnaces and basements first.

Spring brings thunderstorms and sometimes tornadoes.

The terrain adds a second factor. The village sits in wooded marshland where several streams begin. Most drain to Salt Creek, which rises at Wilke Marsh on the east side, while the northeast corner drains to Buffalo Creek and a small piece of the southeast to McDonald Creek. Wet basements, sump pumps and grading are therefore routine inspection topics. If your house has had water in the basement, a buyer will want to see repair records and any permit for drainage work.

  • Finishing or remodeling a basement, kitchen or bathroom.

Where is Hoffman Estates, Illinois, and where did the village come from?

Hoffman Estates is a village in the northwest suburbs, mostly in Cook County with a very small part in Kane County. Of its 21.07 square miles, nearly all is dry land, and mail is delivered under ZIP codes 60169, 60010 and 60192.

German settlers had farmed the area west of Roselle Road and north of Golf Road, then called Wildcat Grove. In 1954 Sam and Jack Hoffman, a father and son who ran a construction company, bought 160 acres and began building homes. Residents voted to incorporate, and the village was incorporated on September 23, 1959. Annexations north of the Northwest Tollway in the early 1960s more than doubled its land area.

The village had 22,238 people in 1970 and 52,530 in the 2020 census. The count rose from 8,296 in 1960 to 46,363 in 1990, so many houses are several decades old, and a buyer will ask how old the roof, furnace and windows are.

What do federal housing figures say about Hoffman Estates?

QuickFacts estimates 50,858 residents in mid-2025, which is 3.2 percent below the April 2020 base. The 2020 to 2024 survey counts 18,537 households of about 2.75 people each. Of the homes, 74.2 percent are owned, and those owners report a median value of $351,900. Renters pay a median gross rent of $1,734, and the middle household income is $106,806.

Two other numbers stand out: 35.4 percent of residents were born abroad, and 46.4 percent of people 5 and older use a non-English language at home. In the year before the survey, 90.5 percent stayed at one address.

  • Just over a quarter of homes have renters, so investor-owned and tenant-occupied houses come up in sales.
  • With so many languages spoken, translated showing instructions and listing documents can help.
  • The 2020 count listed 19,160 housing units, and 3.5 percent were vacant.

What jobs and businesses drive the local economy?

The Prairie Stone Business Park, a 750-acre planned district bounded by Illinois Route 59, Interstate 90, Illinois Route 72 and Beverly Road, anchors the village's employment. It took shape after Sears relocated its headquarters there in 1993, and it later added the 11,000-seat NOW Arena, a Marriott hotel and the Poplar Creek Crossing retail center. The Village took over the arena in 2011, and it is home to the Windy City Bulls of the NBA G League. The park also holds a Northern Illinois University branch, a health and wellness center and offices for companies such as Serta, Mary Kay and I-CAR.

A 2023 list of top local employers starts with St. Alexius Medical Center at 2,500 workers, then Siemens Medical Systems and Claire's at 400 each, the Village itself at 370, and FANUC America and Vistex at 350 each. Many Japanese companies also base their U.S. headquarters in Hoffman Estates and neighboring Schaumburg.

A transfer or job change can force a quick sale. Commutes average 28.5 minutes, and Woodfield Mall in neighboring Schaumburg, opened in 1971, turned the area into a major business center.

Which school districts serve Hoffman Estates?

Several districts overlap here, so the assigned school follows the street address.

  • North of Interstate 90, Township High School District 211 serves high school students.
  • In that northern area, Community Consolidated School District 15 (K to 8) serves addresses east of Huntington Boulevard.
  • Barrington School District 220 (K to 12) serves addresses west of Huntington Boulevard in the same area.
  • Residents west of Barrington Road primarily attend Elgin Area U46.

Most of the village is in Harper College Community College District 512. Libraries that serve residents include the Schaumburg Township District Library, the Barrington Area Library, the Gail Borden Public Library District and the Palatine Township Library. Pace runs bus routes that connect the village to Elgin, Rosemont and other destinations.

Confirm the district for your exact address before you name any school in a listing.

What does Village Hall require before a Hoffman Estates sale can close?

The Village's transfer tax dates to 1987 and falls on the seller of any real estate sold or transferred inside Village limits. Payment and the stamp come before closing and recording, and the Village prints the cost as $3 per $1,000 of the selling price.

  • Allow 48 hours of notice so staff can process the stamp, and send applications or questions to transferstamps@vohe.org.
  • Bring the state transfer declaration (PTAX-203/EZ Dec) and the deed or other document going to the recorder.
  • Call the Water Department at 847-843-4824 at least five days before buying the stamp to order a final water bill.
  • Call 847-882-9100 or use that same email to confirm no liens or fines remain on the property and the garbage bill is paid.
  • An exempt stamp costs a $10.00 administrative fee, needs the fully executed deed carrying the exempt language and signature, and calls for a final water reading if ownership changes.

Stamps are sold at the Village Hall front counter at 1900 Hassell Road on weekdays during business hours, or by mail with a self-addressed stamped return envelope. Settle with your closing agent who will buy the stamp and on what day. Stamp questions go to 847-882-9100.

Where does a Hoffman Estates deed get filed, and what do Cook County and the state charge?

Most of the village sits in Cook County, so deeds go to the Cook County Clerk's recordings division at 118 N. Clark Street. The Clerk's fee page prices a deed at $107, which bundles the county recording fee, a GIS fee, a document storage fee, the State Rental Housing Support Fee and a non-government filer fee. Mail-in recording with return adds $5 per document.

In the Clerk's transfer fee table, the seller is liable for two more charges: .50 per $500.00 for the State of Illinois and .25 per $500.00 for Cook County. The statute behind the state tax is 35 ILCS 200/31-10.

Pick based on how much time and repair work you can take on.

  • Market the house openly. Exposure is greatest, though the sale then rides on the buyer's loan, appraisal and inspection.

What are your options for a quick house sale in Romeoville?

Romeoville sellers choose between a conventional listing, a sale without an agent, and a direct sale to a buyer who pays cash. The cash route shortens the timeline most, though the village's clearance letter and transfer stamp process applies to every sale. Plan for it early, because the clearance letter expires after five business days.

This page covers Romeoville's setting, the housing numbers, and the local steps that sit between a contract and a recorded deed.

  • A listing exposes the house to the largest pool of buyers and the slowest closing.
  • A private sale avoids commission and leaves marketing and negotiation to you.
  • A direct sale to a cash buyer is typically as-is, with a closing date set by the seller.

What is Romeoville like for a house seller?

Romeoville is a village in Will County, about 26 miles southwest of Chicago, on the Gateway Wetlands just west of the Des Plaines River and Historic U.S. Route 66, now IL-53. It sits between Bolingbrook and Joliet near Interstates 55 and 355. The village was incorporated on January 19, 1895, after residents of the river port of Romeo voted to change the name, and it covers about 20 square miles.

The area earned the nickname Stone City because of its limestone quarries, and stone from Romeoville was used to build the Illinois State Capitol in Springfield. Lewis University was founded on the edge of town in 1934. In 1950 the village had roughly 46 homes. The Hampton Park Subdivision began in 1957 on more than 600 acres of wetland along IL-53, and the 1990 opening of the Weber Road interchange on I-55 set off two decades of rapid building. Population rose from 21,153 in 2000 to 39,680 in 2010.

Romeoville's ZIP codes are 60446 and 60491, and its land falls across four townships: DuPage, Lockport, Plainfield and Wheatland.

What do the Census numbers say about homes in Romeoville?

QuickFacts estimates 41,281 residents on July 1, 2025, up 1.2% from the April 2020 base. Housing here skews toward ownership: 80.7% of units are owner-occupied, and households average 3.05 people across 13,296 households.

Where do Romeoville residents work?

The village website lists Amazon as the largest employer at 1,824 workers, followed by Valley View School District 365U at 1,300, Green Core at 1,200 and the CITGO refinery operation at 803. Aryzta, Ulta Beauty, Walmart, Magid Glove and Safety and Lewis University each employ more than 500. Kehe Foods and FedEx Ground are also named as major employers.

Romeoville is home to over 600 businesses and won a Gold Medal from the International Economic Development Council in 2013 for adding 1,560 jobs over 2012 and 2013. Warehouse, refinery and retail employers sit close to I-55, so a house with easy access to that interchange gives a buyer a shorter drive to those jobs.

Which schools serve Romeoville?

Many Romeoville students attend Valley View School District 365U, which includes Romeoville High School, A. Vito Martinez Middle School, John J. Lukancic Middle School and elementary schools named for Beverly Skoff, Irene King, Kenneth L. Hermansen and Robert C. Hill. Some neighborhoods lie in other districts: students may attend Plainfield East High School or Lockport Township High School.

For college, Lewis University has its main campus on the village's edge, and Joliet Junior College and Rasmussen College both run campuses in Romeoville. Since district lines cross the village, confirm the school assignment for a specific address before quoting it to a buyer.

What must happen at the Village of Romeoville before a closing?

Romeoville's Real Estate Transfer Tax is the buyer's responsibility, but the seller has to clear the property first. To get a transfer stamp, the property must be clear of all debts to the village, including the most current water bill. You request a clearance letter, which starts the process and orders a final water reading. Clearance letters are valid for five business days. A final meter reading is not required for an exempt transaction if the water account is in good standing and the name stays the same.

The village prints its tax as $3.50 per $1,000 of the full consideration price for nonexempt transactions, or a $40 processing fee for exempt ones. Payment can be made online by credit card or e-check, or in person. After payment, you get a receipt with space for the stamp, and the physical stamp can be handed over or mailed. A lost stamp must be repurchased at full price.

A refund is available only to residents who sell the home they live in and buy another Romeoville home as a new principal residence, within 12 months of each other. The Finance Department is at 1050 W Romeo Road, phone 815-886-7212.

How does the final water bill work in Romeoville?

The final water bill is part of the clearance. The village mails it to the forwarding address you provide after closing. The seller's account stays in the seller's name until a final on-site meter read is complete, so give the Water Billing office your closing date and mailing address in advance.

Any unpaid balance blocks the stamp, which in turn blocks recording. Paying the account in full the day the reading posts keeps the closing on schedule.

What state and county stamps does a Romeoville deed need?

State law sets the Illinois stamp at 50 cents per $500 of value or fraction, sold through the county recorder (35 ILCS 200/31-15). A deed will not be accepted for filing unless those stamps have been purchased from the recorder of the county where it is filed (35 ILCS 200/31-20). Romeoville is in Will County, so the recording office there handles the filing. Ask the Will County Clerk's recording office for its current fee schedule and the county stamp amount, because those figures are set by the county.

Your title company normally prepares the state transfer declaration and delivers the deed with the village stamp attached.

How does Will County bill property tax, and what does a seller owe?

Will County mails bills on May 1 for the previous tax year, and the Treasurer's levy calendar for bills paid in 2026 shows a first installment due June 1, 2026 and a second due September 1, 2026, both with postmarks accepted. Late payments accrue interest under state statute: 1.5% per month on the first installment starting June 2, with the rate stepping up in later months.

For a seller, the practical step is to check whether both installments are paid and to settle the proration on the closing statement. The calendar changes yearly, so ask the Will County Treasurer for the schedule that applies to your sale.

Who pays the transfer tax in Romeoville?

The buyer is responsible for Romeoville's Real Estate Transfer Tax. The village prints $3.50 per $1,000 of full consideration for nonexempt transactions and a $40 fee for exempt ones, but the seller must still clear village debts first.

How long is a Romeoville clearance letter good for?

Five business days. The letter starts the clearance process and orders the final water reading, so request it close to your closing date.

Do I need a final water reading when I sell in Romeoville?

Usually yes. A final reading is not required for an exempt transaction if the account is in good standing and the name on it stays the same. For a normal sale the seller's account stays open until a final on-site read, and the last bill is mailed to your forwarding address.

Can I get a transfer tax refund in Romeoville?

Only if you live in the home, sell it, and buy another Romeoville home as your new principal residence within 12 months. Owner-occupants who sell and buy outside the village do not qualify.

Which county records a Romeoville deed?

Will County. The deed goes to the Will County recording office with the state and county stamps and the village stamp. Your title company usually files it.

Where is Park Ridge and how did it develop?

Park Ridge is a city in Cook County about 15 miles north of downtown Chicago, close to O'Hare International Airport. It covers roughly 7 square miles and touches three Chicago community areas on the Far Northwest Side: Edison Park, Norwood Park and O'Hare. The Des Plaines River separates it from Des Plaines to the west.

The ground itself shaped the early town. Clay deposits fed a brickworks that George Penny established in 1854, and locals called the settlement Brickton, after an earlier name of Pennyville. The city was incorporated in 1873. Population then jumped from 10,417 in 1930 to 32,659 in 1960 and peaked at 42,614 in 1970 before settling near 39,656 in the 2020 census. Much of the housing stock traces to that mid-century boom, so a buyer's inspector will look closely at the age of the wiring, plumbing, roof and foundation.

What do the Census numbers say about Park Ridge homeowners?

Park Ridge is a city of long-time owners. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates show 92.8 percent of residents living in the same house a year earlier.

With 84.8 percent of units owner-occupied, most buyers are likely to be families who plan to live in the house and who usually rely on a mortgage. A house that cannot pass a lender's appraisal or an inspection can lose that kind of buyer, which is where a cash sale enters the picture.

How do the trains and schools affect a Park Ridge sale?

Two Metra stops, Park Ridge and Dee Road, sit on the Union Pacific Northwest Line, with service southeast to Ogilvie Transportation Center and northwest to Harvard and McHenry. The CTA runs Route 68 to Chicago, and Pace operates several regional routes.

Schools are a major reason families look here:

  • Park Ridge-Niles School District 64 runs the elementary schools, including Carpenter, Field, Franklin, Roosevelt and Washington, plus Lincoln Middle School and Emerson Middle School in Niles.
  • Maine Township High School District 207 serves high school students. Maine East and Maine South are the two campuses, and students in the north part of the city can choose either.
  • St. Paul of the Cross and Mary Seat of Wisdom are the Catholic elementary schools, and St. Andrews is Lutheran.
  • The city belongs to the Oakton Community College district.

The city's 2020 financial report lists Advocate Lutheran General Hospital as its largest employer, with 3,693 employees, followed by the high school district, the Park District and District 64.

Do you need a permit for repairs on a Park Ridge house?

A permit is required for most construction. The city lists new buildings, additions, garages, driveways, HVAC, electrical and plumbing work, pools, fences, patios, decks, sheds and siding. It does not require one for window replacement unless the opening is enlarged, or for residential roof replacement, although roofing contractors must be licensed with the city. Routine maintenance that leaves existing systems and structural walls alone also needs none.

Timing matters if you plan fixes before a sale:

  • Reviews usually take up to two weeks, and the standard time is two weeks for every permit during the May to September busy season.
  • Residential permits stay valid for one year, and a renewal after expiration costs 50 percent of the original permit fee.
  • Applications go through the Civic Access online portal, and inspections are booked by morning or afternoon block with a one to two business day lead time.

Questions go to the Community Preservation and Development department at 847-318-5291. A separate tree removal permit is required for trees larger than 10 inches in diameter, so check before clearing a lot.

What does the Park Ridge transfer tax cost and who files it?

The city charges its own real estate transfer tax, and the seller pays it. The city's FAQ prints the rate as $2.00 per $1,000 of value or fraction thereof. Cook County Clerk's municipal list shows the same rate for Park Ridge, notes that it includes foreclosures, and lists the exempt-transfer fee as $25.00.

To get the transfer tax certificate, send the Finance Department:

  • The PTAX-203 or MyDec form.
  • A photo of the water meter for the final reading.
  • The closing date.
  • A contact name, phone number and email address.

Documents go to transferstamp@parkridge.us or to the Finance Department at 505 Butler Place; questions go to 847-318-5222, option 4. The certificate is issued once the tax and any other amounts owed to the city, including the final water bill, are paid, and the certificate is attached to the deed at recording. Cook County adds its own state rate of 50 cents per $500 and county rate of 25 cents per $500.

How do water bills and closing dates work in Park Ridge?

The city bills water every other month, with bills issued on the last day of the month and due by the 20th. Email the meter photo no earlier than five days before closing, with the service address and closing date. Water is not shut off during a transfer, and the account moves automatically into the buyer's name.

Final payment is accepted as cash, credit or debit card, certified check, money order or attorney's check. Homeowners are responsible for repairs to the water service pipe between the buffalo box and the house, which is worth knowing if a buyer's inspection turns up a leak. The city also says property assessment is a Cook County function, so appeals and exemptions go to the county assessor, not City Hall.

Are there landmark or preservation rules to know about?

Park Ridge has a Historic Preservation Commission. According to the city's FAQ, a house becomes a local landmark only with the owner's consent, and a designation can be rescinded, though the Commission encourages owners to look at alternatives first. If your house is already landmarked, tell buyers early.

What are your options for selling quickly in Park Ridge?

With a median owner-occupied value of $551,200 and owners who tend to stay put, a standard listing is the usual route when a house is in good shape. A cash buyer is more useful when the house needs work that would take months to finish, when a probate or move deadline is close, or when you want to avoid showings.

Before you accept any offer, line up the transfer tax certificate steps above, because closing cannot be completed without the city's certificate and the final water reading. Ask your closing attorney or title company to start those steps as soon as the contract is signed.

The city's FAQ prints it as $2.00 per $1,000 of value or fraction thereof, paid by the seller. Cook County's clerk list matches that rate. The state adds 50 cents per $500 and the county adds 25 cents per $500.

Do I need to pay my final water bill before closing in Park Ridge?

Yes. The transfer tax certificate is issued after the tax and any other amounts owed to the city, including the final water bill, are paid. Email a photo of the meter to the Finance Department no earlier than five days before closing.

Can I replace my roof or windows in Park Ridge without a permit?

Usually yes. The city says residential roof replacement and window replacement do not need a permit, unless the window opening is enlarged. Roofing contractors must be licensed with the city, and other projects such as decks, fences and electrical work still require permits.

Who handles Park Ridge property tax appeals?

Cook County does. The city says assessment is a county function and refers owners to the Cook County Assessor's office, which handles appeals, exemptions and the required forms.

Does the water account transfer when a Park Ridge house sells?

Yes. The city places the account in the buyer's name automatically, does not shut off service during the transfer, and bills every other month afterward. Sellers settle the final reading through the transfer tax process.

Where is Pekin and what is its housing like?

Pekin is the county seat of Tazewell County, on the Illinois River in central Illinois. It is the largest city in the county and the second most populous in the Peoria metropolitan area. A small part of the city lies in Peoria County, reached by a bridge over the river, which means some Pekin addresses are recorded and taxed in a different county than most of the city.

The Census Bureau counted 31,731 residents in 2020, down from 34,094 in 2010, and estimated 31,277 for July 2025. Housing here costs far less than in the Chicago suburbs: the median owner-occupied value in Palatine, for comparison, is $355,600. The table shows what the 2020 to 2024 figures look like for owners and renters.

What is Pekin's history and why does it matter to a seller?

A settler from Ohio built a log cabin on a ridge above the river in 1824, and a surveyor laid out the town site in 1827. One account says the name Pekin came from a nineteenth-century habit of naming towns after places thought to lie on the opposite side of the globe. The first post office opened in 1832.

Coal mining left a physical mark. Wikipedia lists at least four mines: the Pekin, Regal, Tazewell and Ubben mines. One of them, run by the Pekin Coal Mining Company until 1952, lay under what later became Broadmoor Junior High, Willow Elementary and Schramm School. The Regal mine crossed Broadway in the eastern part of town, below what is now Parkway Golf Course and Coal Miner's Park. Coal mining in Pekin had ended by 1951.

If a buyer asks whether your lot sits over old workings, the title company or the county recorder's records are the place to start. Do not guess at the answer in a listing.

Which employers and schools shape the Pekin market?

Pekin is home to the headquarters of Pekin Insurance and to the Federal Correctional Institution, Pekin, and it has its own hospital, Carle Health Peoria - Pekin Hospital. CityLink buses on Routes 17, 18 and 23 connect the city to downtown Peoria. The Census Bureau puts the average commute at 21.7 minutes.

Public schools depend on where the house sits:

  • Most of the city is in Pekin Public School District 108, which has six elementary schools, two intermediate schools, two junior highs and the Pekin Technical Education Center.
  • Parts of the Tazewell County side belong instead to North Pekin-Marquette Heights School District 102 or Rankin Community School District 98.
  • All of Pekin in Tazewell County feeds Pekin Community High School District 303.
  • The Peoria County portion is in Hollis Consolidated School District 328 and Limestone Community High School District 310.

Ask the district for the boundary of your address before a buyer does.

How do Pekin's weather and river location affect a house?

Pekin has a hot-summer continental climate. NOAA normals for 1991 to 2020 show about 37.4 inches of precipitation a year, spread through the seasons with late spring the wettest, January afternoons near 33 degrees and July afternoons near 86. Summers are humid, and winters can turn severely cold and snowy.

The river adds a flood question. The city takes part in the National Flood Insurance Program and says properties below the 1 percent annual chance flood level may be required by law to carry flood insurance. An owner who thinks the flood designation is wrong can ask FEMA for a Letter of Map Amendment, and lenders may still require insurance. Properties along the Illinois River are often subject to floodway rules. For a sale, find out your flood zone early, since it affects a buyer's mortgage and insurance.

What does Pekin require for permits and yard rules before a sale?

Pekin's Inspections Department says permits are required for electrical, plumbing, sewer, heating, ventilation and air conditioning work, and also for fences, sheds, new homes, additions, decks, signs and pools. A roofing permit applies to a complete tear-off or a second layer of shingles. Siding, windows, doors and interior remodeling need none unless the work changes structural walls, plumbing or electrical.

Other rules a buyer's agent may bring up:

  • A homeowner may do their own work but must still get a permit. The city defines a homeowner as the person who owns and lives at the residence.
  • Pools deeper than 24 inches need a permit and may sit only in the rear yard.
  • Chain link fences are not allowed in any front yard, and corner lots must keep sight lines clear.
  • Vehicles may not be parked in yards or the right of way, and must stand on a hard surface such as concrete or asphalt.

The Inspections Department takes questions at 309.478.5364. If you built a deck or finished a basement without a permit, ask whether it can be inspected before you list.

Which county records a Pekin deed, and who collects the taxes?

Most Pekin parcels are in Tazewell County, where the County Clerk and Recorder keeps real estate records. The office says everything in the Recorder's files is public record, that anyone may look through it free of charge, and that it supplies some forms at no cost. Ask the office for current recording fees and transfer stamp amounts before closing, since they change.

Parcels in the Peoria County portion go through Peoria County instead. That county's land records page says it participates in the state's MyDec system, which lets filers submit the PTAX-203 transfer declaration electronically before a deed is recorded. Check your tax bill or parcel number to see which county applies, and tell your closing attorney if the house straddles the line.

How do homeowners sell quickly in Pekin?

The median value of owner-occupied homes in Pekin is $120,700, so repair costs can take a large share of the price. A new roof or furnace is a bigger decision when the house is worth a fraction of what homes cost in Chicago's suburbs. For that reason many sellers weigh a cash purchase against listing and fixing the house first.

  • Pull any permits or inspection records so a buyer can see what was done.
  • Confirm your flood zone and your school district boundary.
  • Ask the title company which county records your parcel and whether any liens or unpaid taxes are on file.
  • Compare offers by what you keep after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not by headline price.

Which county is Pekin in?

Pekin is the county seat of Tazewell County. A small part of the city extends into Peoria County, so parcels there are recorded and taxed through Peoria County. Check your parcel number to see which applies.

Do I need a permit to replace a roof in Pekin?

Yes, for a complete tear-off and replacement, or for adding a second layer of shingles. The city's Inspections Department says siding, window and door replacement do not need a permit unless structural, plumbing or electrical changes are involved.

Does Pekin have flood rules that affect a sale?

Yes. The city takes part in the National Flood Insurance Program, and properties below the 1 percent annual chance flood level may be required by law to carry flood insurance. New construction in a flood hazard area must set the lowest floor two feet above base flood elevation.

Can I do my own repairs on my Pekin house?

Yes, if you own and live in it, but you still need the permit. The city defines a homeowner as the person who owns and lives at the residence, and nobody may work on someone else's property unless licensed or registered with the Inspections Department.

Where do I get recording information for a Pekin sale?

Ask the Tazewell County Clerk and Recorder, whose office keeps real estate records open to the public at no charge and supplies some forms for free. For the Peoria County portion of the city, use the Peoria County land records office, which accepts the MyDec transfer declaration.

Where is Highland Park, Illinois, and what shapes the housing here?

Highland Park is a city in Lake County on the North Shore of the Chicago area, about 25 miles north of downtown Chicago. Its 12.24 square miles of dry land are split between Moraine Township and West Deerfield Township, and mail goes through ZIP codes 60035, 60036 and 60037.

Lake Michigan defines the layout. A bluff about 100 feet high runs along 6 miles of shoreline, and wooded ravines cut up to a mile inland. Elevations range from 580 to 725 feet above sea level. A house beside a ravine or at the bluff edge sells differently from one on a flat street near a Metra stop, and buyers of every kind will ask about the lot as closely as the building.

In the 2020 count the city had 11,557 households spread over 12,405 housing units, and 6.8 percent of those units stood empty. A mid-2025 estimate puts the population at 30,767.

How did Highland Park grow, and why do so many older houses survive?

Two small lakefront settlements, St. John's and Port Clinton, came first. After the Chicago and Milwaukee Railroad built a depot, a plat was laid out in 1856. Highland Park was established as a city on March 11, 1869, and it annexed the village of Ravinia in 1899. St. Johns Avenue and Port Clinton Square still carry the old settlement names.

The housing stock reflects that early start. The Willits House is on the federal historic register, and the register also lists, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright, along with homes by John S. Van Bergen, Howard Van Doren Shaw, Robert E. Seyfarth and David Adler. Landscape architect Jens Jensen lived in the city and designed projects that are on the register as well.

Owners of an architect-designed house usually have the original plans, permits and drawings in a drawer somewhere. Gather them before you talk to any buyer, because documented history is the one thing that can set a house apart from its neighbors.

How common is homeownership in Highland Park, by the federal numbers?

The five-year survey figures cover 2020 to 2024. They give Highland Park 11,787 households, 83.8 percent of them owners, and a median home value of $607,300. Renters pay a median gross rent of $1,925. Roughly 87.5 percent of residents stayed at the same address through the previous year, and 24.3 percent are 65 or older.

Those numbers describe a city of long-time owners. Downsizing, estate settlement and relocation all produce sales with a firm deadline. Median household income is $168,094, and workers travel 27.5 minutes on average to get to a job.

  • Because most residents stay put, your listing may be the first on the street in years, so pull recent sale records before you pick a price.
  • Older construction makes for a long inspection report, and a buyer may ask to see original plans and permits.
  • Four Metra stations inside city limits make distance to the platform a selling point for downtown workers.

Which schools and commuting routes matter to Highland Park buyers?

Public schools come from two districts. North Shore School District 112 operates an early childhood center, seven elementary schools and two middle schools. Township High School District 113 operates Highland Park High School and also Deerfield High School in nearby Deerfield.

US 41 is the main highway and connects Chicago to Milwaukee. Four Metra stations sit inside the city limits: Braeside, Ravinia Park, Ravinia and Highland Park. All are on the Union Pacific North Line, which starts in Chicago and ends in Kenosha, Wisconsin. Pace buses add local routes, O'Hare is about 20 miles southwest, and the Skokie Valley Trail runs through town.

Ravinia, the open-air pavilion that seats 3,200, has been the summer home of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra since 1936. Three public beaches, Rosewood, Moraine and Park Avenue, round out the lakefront. Buyers of every type, cash buyers included, weigh the stations, schools and beaches when they set a price.

What must happen at City Hall before a Highland Park closing?

Chapter 97, Article X of the city code taxes real property transfers. The declaration form prints the rate as $5.00 per $1,000 or fraction thereof of full actual consideration, and it puts payment on the transferor when the sale contract says nothing different.

  • The declaration needs a signature from a transferor and a transferee.
  • A final water bill must be prepared and paid when the tax stamp is bought, and a final meter reading can be scheduled up to five business days before closing.
  • A copy of the deed headed for the Recorder of Deeds goes to the city, while an exempt transfer requires the original.
  • Consideration counts the mortgage amount and any liabilities the buyer assumes.
  • Section 97.1004 lists exempt deeds. Examples include tax deeds, partition deeds, deeds with consideration under $100, and foreclosure or in-lieu deeds to a mortgage holder.

The form says personal checks and credit cards are refused. Finance, at 1707 St. Johns Avenue, takes calls at 847.432.0800 and email at Finance@cityhpil.com.

What does the Lake County Clerk charge to record a Highland Park deed?

The Recording Division of the Lake County Clerk's Office handles deeds at 18 N County Street, 6th Floor, Waukegan, phone 847-377-2575. Its fee page sets $70 for a standard document and $82 for a non-standard one, and says state and county transfer taxes are the only added charges at recording.

The state levies its own tax under 35 ILCS 200/31-10, charged on the value stated in the declaration, and a mortgage the buyer takes over can be excluded when the deed says so. The closing agent will give you the county rate and a final total.

Which selling route fits a Highland Park owner in a hurry?

Three routes exist, and each trades price, certainty and effort differently.

  • Work with a listing agent. Exposure is widest, and a bluff, ravine or architect-designed property can justify a longer wait.
  • Go it alone. You control the contract and carry the showings, disclosures and negotiation.
  • Accept a cash offer. The closing date can follow your calendar and the house stays as it is, which helps with an estate home, a tenant-occupied unit or a house that needs work.

The city stamp, the final water bill and the deed filing apply on every route. Ask for the final reading early so closing does not wait on a meter.

When a cash buyer makes an offer, get in writing who pays each transfer charge named above. The sale contract is where the allocation is settled.

How many people live in Highland Park?

The April 2020 census found 30,176 residents, and the Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 30,767.

Who owes the city transfer tax on a Highland Park sale?

The transferor does, as the city's form reads, when the contract has no clause to the contrary.

Does a Highland Park sale need a final water bill?

Yes. The form requires it to be prepared and paid when the stamp is bought, and a final meter reading can be booked up to five business days ahead of closing.

Which office files the deed after a Highland Park closing?

The Lake County Clerk's Recording Division in Waukegan. Its published fee for a standard document is $70.

Which school districts serve Highland Park?

North Shore School District 112 runs the elementary and middle schools, and Township High School District 113 runs Highland Park High School and Deerfield High School.

Where is Huntley, Illinois, and why does it sit in two counties?

Huntley is a village in the northwest Chicago area that straddles McHenry County and Kane County. It lies along Interstate 90, covers about 14.29 square miles of land, and uses ZIP code 60142. Three townships divide it: Grafton, Rutland and Hampshire.

The village's own FAQ gives the township split. Land north of Kreutzer Road is in Grafton Township, and land south of Kreutzer Road is in Rutland Township, except the northwest end of Sun City, which is in Hampshire Township. The county and township matter to a seller because they decide which office handles your tax bill and your deed.

Huntley was founded in 1851 and incorporated in 1872, and it is named for Thomas Stillwell Huntley. Its census count was 5,730 in 2000, 24,291 in 2010 and 27,740 in 2020, one of the sharpest growth curves in the region.

What do the Census numbers say about Huntley homeowners?

The Census Bureau estimated 29,132 residents on July 1, 2025, up 5.0 percent from the April 2020 base. Median household income is $88,536, and the mean commute is 29.5 minutes.

The age profile is the most unusual part. QuickFacts lists 34.1 percent of residents as 65 or older and only 3.2 percent under 5. The 2020 census put the median age at 48.2.

What drives the local economy and the roads around Huntley?

Growth in new businesses and distribution warehouses, especially along Illinois Route 47, has shaped the last decade. A small downtown keeps restaurants and shops. Route 47 is the main north-south road and runs nearly seven miles through the village. It was widened from two to five lanes in 2011, carries over 20,000 vehicles a day, and meets I-90 at a full interchange that was finished in November 2013.

Algonquin Road, a four-lane divided highway, runs east toward Algonquin and Lake in the Hills, and Main Street connects west toward Marengo and Harmony Road. Huntley-Dundee Road leads east to the Carpentersville and Dundee area. The Union Pacific Belvidere Subdivision passes through, and many local industries sit near the tracks.

Huntley once planned a stop on a proposed Metra intercity line from Rockford to Chicago, but it withdrew over concerns about its downtown. A listing can point to the I-90 and Route 47 access as a practical selling point.

Which schools and services come with a Huntley address?

Huntley Community School District 158 serves the village. Huntley High School is on Harmony Road, and the middle schools are Marlowe in Lake in the Hills and Heineman in Algonquin. Elementary schools include Leggee in Huntley, Martin and Chesak in Lake in the Hills, and Conley and Mackeben in Algonquin.

  • The Huntley Fire Protection District covers about 55 square miles and serves all village residents.
  • The Huntley Area Public Library is on Ruth Road. The Hampshire Township part of the village is served by the Ella Johnson Memorial Public Library.
  • The Huntley Park District runs the recreation center on Mill Street.

  • Watering follows a four-tier color-coded conservation program (red, yellow, orange and green), with signs posted around the village.

  • A garage sale needs no permit, though signs may go only on private property.

Starting that permit at least two weeks before closing keeps the date from slipping.

What kind of village is Round Lake Beach?

Round Lake Beach is a village in northern Lake County, incorporated on February 5, 1937, and covers about 5.2 square miles. The 2020 census counted 27,252 residents, down from 28,175 in 2010. It is the principal city of the Round Lake Beach, McHenry and Grayslake urban area, which had 261,835 people in 2020, and the village has the second highest Latino population in Lake County after Waukegan.

Population grew from 1,892 in 1950 to 25,859 in 2000, so the housing stock reflects building over several decades. Major streets include Monaville Road, Fairfield Road, Rollins Road, Cedar Lake Road, Hook Drive and Hainesville Road.

The village spends roughly $3 million to $4 million a year on infrastructure improvements using tax increment financing and motor fuel tax money, according to Wikipedia.

What do Census figures say about Round Lake Beach homes?

How do commuting and jobs affect demand in Round Lake Beach?

The village has a station on Metra's North Central Service, which runs between Antioch and Chicago Union Station on weekdays. Pace Route 570 connects Round Lake Beach with Fox Lake, Grayslake and other points. Census data puts the mean commute at 30.4 minutes, and 72.9% of residents 16 and older are in the labor force.

The train station and the road links along Rollins Road and Cedar Lake Road are the usual selling points for a commuter. Households here are large, at 3.16 people each, so family-sized houses are the norm.

Which school district serves Round Lake Beach?

Round Lake Area School District 116 serves the village and four other communities. The district reports about 6,000 students, 10 schools and roughly 1,000 staff members, with a four-year graduation rate of 88% for 2024. Round Lake High School reopened in 2016 after a renovation that added 27 learning lab classrooms, science labs and a new gymnasium.

The district opened a school-based health center in 2014 in partnership with the Lake County Health Department and runs an in-district preschool program for about 200 students. Families asking about schools usually want to know the attendance boundary for one address, which the district can confirm.

What is the occupancy permit, and when do you need it?

Round Lake Beach requires every residential property to obtain an Occupancy Permit before it is sold. The permit moves water and sewer service from the seller to the buyer and confirms the exterior is maintained and up to code. The village asks you to contact it at least two weeks before closing.

  • Fill out the online occupancy application, select the address and choose the Occupancy permit type.
  • Attach photos of the water meter.
  • After the application is accepted, pay the $60 fee by emailed link.
  • The inspection is scheduled after payment. It covers the exterior only, and no one has to be present.
  • Five days before closing, email a photo of the inside meter reading and the outside receiver reading, if there is one, so the final water bill can be calculated.

The village's FAQs add that the final water bill must be paid before the buyers can pick up the occupancy certificate. Call the Finance Department at 847-546-2351 as soon as the closing date is set.

How do water bills and deposits work during a sale?

Water and sewer bills go out every two months, in January, March, May, July, September and November, and a bill unpaid after its due date can carry a 10% late fee under the village FAQ. New owners pay a $100 deposit billed on the first bill, refundable only after ownership or tenancy changes and the final bill is paid in full.

The village's billing page lists its water and sewer charges per 1,000 gallons plus per-bill customer and sewer fees, and it adds a phosphorus surcharge for regional treatment at the Fox Lake facility. Rates have been adjusted in 2026, so ask Village Hall for the schedule that applies to your final bill.

What if the house is a rental?

Rental owners follow a separate annual certification program. Landlords receive a notice in early to mid October with their inspection times, deadlines and fees. Requirements include a submitted application, the certification fee, a passed inspection with deficiencies resolved, current Crime Free certification, and no outstanding liens or payments owed to the village. Missing the deadline brings a $100 late fee and a two-week extension, and after that the property can go to adjudication with an additional $1,500 fine and liens.

Landlords new to the village must attend a Crime-Free Housing seminar, or show proof of certification from another Chicagoland municipality. Call 847-546-2351 for seminar information. A seller with tenants should confirm the certification is current before accepting a contract.

What transfer taxes and property tax dates apply in Round Lake Beach?

The Lake County Clerk's Recording Division collects the state and county transfer taxes at recording: 50 cents per $500 for the state and 25 cents per $500 for the county, issued as a single stamp. The county's pamphlet says the tax may be paid by buyer or seller, so check your contract. A state transfer declaration (PTAX-203) accompanies the deed unless an exemption statement is signed. Do I need an occupancy permit to sell in Round Lake Beach?

Yes. Residential properties must obtain an Occupancy Permit before sale. The fee is $60 and the inspection covers the exterior only.

At least two weeks before closing. The village also schedules the final water reading about 3 to 5 days before closing, so call the Finance Department at 847-546-2351 once the date is set.

Does anyone need to be home for the inspection?

No. The occupancy inspection is exterior only, and the village says no one is required to be present.

What is the water deposit for new owners?

A $100 deposit billed on the buyer's first water and sewer bill. It is not refundable until the property changes ownership or tenancy and the final bill is paid in full.

Which office records a Round Lake Beach deed?

The Lake County Clerk's Recording Division in Waukegan. It collects the state and county stamps and records the stamped deed.
